analysis.title: Rising yields raise the portfolio appeal of bonds and diversified investing (UBS House View - Daily EMEA)
key_insights: Global bond yields rose last week on recalibrated rate expectations and a rebound in equity appetite. The German 2-year yield rose 12bps, its sharpest weekly rise in two months, and Japanese 10-year yields hit their highest since 22 October, moving with US yields.
The yield rise was linked to news that President Trump was not seeking a peace deal with Iran, and to Fed President Waller's comments on a possible 50bps rate hike at the December Fed meeting.

UBS argues that higher starting yields have restored the case for a traditional 60/40 portfolio. Bonds now offer meaningful income, a larger cushion against further rate rises, potential capital gains if growth slows, and some protection against equity declines.

The 60/40 portfolio is not guaranteed to offset every equity decline. High-quality bonds diversify equities best when inflation is low or stable. If inflation stays elevated and rates rise, stocks and bonds can fall together.

UBS says completion assets suit an uncertain outlook with several plausible paths for growth, inflation, fiscal policy, energy prices and geopolitics. Hedge funds can provide returns when stocks and bonds fall together. Commodities have low correlation with traditional assets and can benefit from supply constraints or high inflation. Private infrastructure may offer predictable, potentially inflation-linked income.

UBS rates high grade and investment grade bonds Attractive and favors short- to medium-duration high-quality bonds. It stays more cautious on the longest maturities because of fiscal concerns and elevated issuance. It also rates high yield and emerging market bonds Attractive on elevated yields and resilient aggregate fundamentals.
Private investments carry illiquidity, limited disclosure, uncertain cash flows, leverage, capital call and blind-pool risks.

A 60/40 US equity-bond portfolio invested in 2020 and left untouched would have drifted to about 80/20 because equities outperformed. UBS recommends regular rebalancing to restore the intended risk profile.

Japan's Q3 GDP contracted at an annualized 0.1%, the first decline in four quarters and worse than the consensus expectation of 0.3% growth. Private consumption fell 0.3% against an expected 0.2% decline, and a large rise in oil imports weighed on trade.

UBS views the Japan weakness as less concerning than the headline. It attributes the consumption fall partly to fading temporary Q2 support from tax and regulatory changes, and the oil import jump to delayed shipments from the prior quarter. It keeps its constructive Japan view and expects the Bank of Japan to raise rates in December 2026 and March 2027.
Calendar for 16 November: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks, and EU industrial production data for September is due.

tension_points.bull_case: If growth weakens and inflation moderates, bond prices may rise as equities come under pressure, so higher starting yields restore the bond cushion and income.
tension_points.bear_case: If inflation remains elevated and interest rates rise, stocks and bonds can decline together, so bonds will not offset every equity decline.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inflation staying elevated with rates still rising, which would make stocks and bonds fall together.

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher starting yields raise income and cushion and improve the case for a 60/40 portfolio.
theme_stances.evidence: elevated starting yields have restored rather than diminished the appeal

theme_stances.key_argument: The Q3 consumption fall reflects fading temporary Q2 support and the oil import jump reflects delayed shipments, so growth should improve.
theme_stances.evidence: we maintain our expectation that the Bank of Japan would raise interest rates further
